classIntro.speaker: Kadam Kyle
classIntro.text:
Hi everyone. I'm just going to say one little thing and then we're going to get on with it. When we do chanted prayers, sometimes our mind is a mess. And this can kind of lead to a complicated situation, which is we're sort of a mess and we're sort of trying to make sense of things and follow along, and then we can kind of get ourselves tied up in knots and then maybe we zone out or whatever, because it's too much. There's lots of different things we can do in those moments, but I'm just going to offer two things that we can do specifically for this case that I've practiced to quite a bit of success when I felt that way.

Thing one is basically make it like a breathing meditation, but with the words of the prayers. So like when you do a breathing meditation, you just try to follow the breath without thinking anything about it. You're just trying to practice concentration. So we can do that with the words. It's like, okay, I can't comprehend anything right now. I can't visualize anything. I can't focus, whatever. I'm just going to try to treat it like a breathing meditation. Not literally focus on the breath, but in the sense of I'm trying to focus. Oop, I get distracted. Okay, let me come back to the words. So this is a really nice strategy because we can do this even if we're a mess. It's like we can do a breathing meditation even if we're a mess. Yeah, it might be messy. We might get distracted a lot, but we're trying. And in that way, it's very beneficial. And sometimes you can really lock in through doing this and a lot of blessings will come through. And even if they don't, at least we have something to do and engage with our mind.

Second thing is just gazing at the Buddhas and essentially just not worrying too much about getting everything right or even following at all. And just gazing at them and just thinking about them a little bit. And you can just think, what was it like for you when you were like me? You know, and it's so cool to think about that. Like, you see Amitayus and you're like, wow, you were Avalokiteshvara's spiritual guide and he's been a Buddha forever. Oh my gosh, you're like ancient. It's just billions and billions and billions of years that you've been a Buddha. Whoa, what was it like when you were like me? You were. You were just practicing and doing your best and trying to get on with things. And then you found Dharma and then you liberated your mind and then you became enlightened. And then eventually you had an incredible student, Avalokiteshvara, who's pervaded so many millions of realms and samsara, really star student, who now posts you up on his head. But it's so cool. Wow, Amitayus, you're amazing. Because he's Amitabha, Amitayus, same person. Wow, you're just so amazing. What was it like to be you, right? And you just feel connected and you think about how cool he is and how amazing he is. And then just the blessings will flow and then we'll get back in some kind of groove. Or Tara or whoever, right?

Or you can even just keep it even less conceptual than that. Like literally just looking. Not even thinking anything else. Like no brain power needed. Like I can't even think right now. I'm just going to stare and let things flow from there. Because the Buddha images are so powerful and so blessed that they'll transform our mind on their own. And so sometimes that's really all we can do. Like if we're really sick, really tired, in a really bad mood, really angry, whatever. It's like, but I've got nothing today. I can't even get up. I'm sideways in bed. I can look at you though. Like that. And we can make that a practice. And it's a completely perfect practice. It's a completely qualified practice just to do that. Without even one ounce more of energy.

So it's just really important for us to know this. I have no idea why I'm sharing this today. I didn't even plan to. Sometimes it's nice to think about little tips and tricks on how to make our chanted prayer practice a little bit better. And it's good to have a plan for when maybe we're not in the zone, or we're tired, or in a mood, or something like that. And to be like, I've got things to do, even in those times. Is that okay? Everyone get those two? So please, especially the second practice of just gazing, it is always a qualified choice. We never have to feel bad about it, or question that, or whatever. It is a more than qualified choice that sometimes we make. And we'll start to see sometimes it's even more profound than us keeping on with the practice. Because there's a depth to it that's very unique. With that in mind, let's begin. Thank you.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments â€” please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful â€” O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and target of remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsaraâ€™s pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharmaâ€™s root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsaraâ€™s ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattvaâ€™s ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the karma path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
You can just imagine or feel that we are in the presence of all the Buddhas. Buddha Shakyamuni in the center, surrounded by countless others, like the full moon surrounded by stars. You can just imagine and feel that infinite light and nectars pour down from all the Buddhas. We just feel our body and mind. We imagine a feeling or sense of peace that arises.

And with this blessing we can reflect on the wish to overcome the self-cherishing mind. We can think, self-cherishing is not me, it is Mara, which is my enemy. It makes me cherish and protect the self I normally see, which does not exist — which is a body and mind pervaded by suffering and delusion. It makes me cherish and want to protect this non-existent self I normally see. It makes me identify, cherish, and protect something that is just the cause of suffering and pain. And it prevents me from identifying with the Buddha's body and mind.

Again, self-cherishing is not us, it is Mara, an inner enemy. It makes us cherish a non-existent self we normally see. It makes us cherish and want to protect an ordinary, suffering, delusion-filled body and mind. And it prevents us from identifying with the Buddha's body and mind.

Just really try to think, I want to overcome this demon of self-cherishing — while thinking very strongly that it is not us. That determination arises, just hold that single-pointedly for the remainder of the meditation. With this determination in mind, it can gradually arise.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Alright, so we will read the root text, Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life. We are moving on to some other verses today. We are kind of one step before the proper purification verses, which are a real treasure. But we won't get into them yet because we are not really on to the confession section. So we will do verse 19 through 27, 19–27. Anyone want to be the reader for today? David, yeah, thank you.

shantidevaReading.speaker: David
shantidevaReading.text:
(19) Eternally I will offer to the Able Ones
Exquisite jewelled parasols held aloft,
With pleasing shapes, handles of gold,
And rims embellished with beautiful ornaments.

(20) In addition to these, may masses of offerings
Resounding with music and beautiful melodies
Remain like so many clouds that send down relief
To suffering living beings.

(21) And upon all the holy Dharma Jewels,
The stupas, and the images,
May there fall an uninterrupted rain
Of flowers, jewels and so forth.

(22) Just as Manjushri, Samantabhadra, and others
Made offerings to the Conquerors,
So do I make offerings to the Sugatas, the Protectors,
And to the Bodhisattvas.

(23) To these oceans of good qualities,
I offer a melodious ocean of praise.
May a chorus of sweet-sounding melodious verses
Always ascend to their presence.

(24) To all the Buddhas abiding in the three times,
The Dharma and the Supreme Assembly,
I prostrate with as many emanated bodies
As there are atoms in all the worlds.

(25) I prostrate to the bases for generating bodhichitta,
To the images of Buddha’s body, speech and mind,
To the Abbots and Preceptors,
And to the supreme practitioners on the path.

(26) Until I attain the essence of great enlightenment,
I will go for refuge to the Buddhas;
Likewise, I will go for refuge to Dharma
And to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

(27) With my palms pressed together, I make requests
To those endowed with great compassion —
The perfect Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas
Who abide throughout the ten directions.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text:
Thank you very much. Alright, so over the last week we were focusing on the practice of offering our body. Could be doing this in all sorts of interesting and lovely ways. But especially this idea of opposing the mind of self-cherishing, which makes us cherish a suffering body and mind — which is the thing that we all are tired of. And the self-cherishing mind makes us obsessed with it and want to protect it all the time. Which is very annoying of it.

And we're also applying the practice in whatever way we'd like. We did talk a little bit about this idea of trying to identify a problem that's associated with self-cherishing and letting that be a motivator for overcoming it. Like a personal problem that feels particularly annoying and frustrating for us, and letting that give us an emotional buy-in to wanting to accomplish it. So it's not just a theory, a theoretical thing, but it is really coming from our own heart. And we also looked at other ways to offer our body, like helping the Dharma Center and more.

Okay, anyone have anything they'd like to share from the week?

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text:
Yesterday, I came here an hour earlier before the fire puja to help out a little bit. And then after a few minutes Kadam Kyle asked me, Ryan, do you have a job? And as soon as I heard the word “job” my miserliness went through the roof. I'm not kidding. Because a job is not like — I knew right away Kadam Kyle is not going to ask me to turn on the lights or turn on the Zoom or take something down. It's a job. It's going to take time. It's going to take away my time or my coffee or whatever. So right away my mind went to a scary, silly mindset. Talking about the pain of miserliness.

Anyhow, he told me, okay, go up and greet people and love people. So I went up and I stand in front of the door and I start greeting whoever came in. At the end, I noticed something. Everyone was sitting, mostly people were sitting and hanging out, everyone was talking. There were three people — one from the Beirut community — standing awkwardly alone, and two others sitting on chairs right next to this but sitting alone. They were not talking to each other. So there's three people who basically don't have anyone to talk to, and they're probably experiencing unpleasant emotions, some kind of isolation.

My mind tells me, Ryan, look away. Don't look at this side of the room. Because technically you're doing your job — you're greeting, you're at the door, you're listening to your teacher. Keep greeting whoever comes in. Look away. Don't look at this side. It's painful. But then I realized, no, that's not what my teacher sent me up for. He said, go up and greet and love people. That's not loving people. So I walked over and I decided to engage all these three and I stood with them until we walked down to the fire puja.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thank you, Ryan. It's great. It's lovely that you were able to practice cherishing others, and it sounds like it was really worthwhile. Right? And helpful for the people who you greeted. Thank you. Anyone else? Dale, yes, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text: So in my meditation this morning I was feeling actually a little bit calmer than I've felt over the last week. I rested a little bit better. So I'm doing my meditation and I start getting interrupted in my mind. And the images of all the Maras that we had on WhatsApp suddenly appear and I felt like I was smacking them away. I just want to smack them out, smack them away. And I continue with my meditation but was getting that — the Maras were really attacking me this morning. And I felt, I mean I was going through especially the meditation part where I was offering my body, offering myself as a servant. They did not like that. So that's what I felt, why they were so strong this morning, coming up and causing me a problem. But I want to go back to what you said when you first started the class, that I think that was very helpful for me — to think about, okay, I did my meditation, so I'm all good, and the heck with the Maras.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, beautiful, thank you, Dale. And you're so right — they particularly don't like when we oppose self-cherishing and self-grasping. That's what the Maras really don't like. Because everything else they can kind of wriggle around with and snuggle into. Even opposing attachment to some degree — because it's like, okay, let's get rid of attachment to that, we'll just get attached to this. Oh, you're not attached to drugs and alcohol and whatever? Okay, now you're attached to your reputation as a Dharma teacher or practitioner. Or now you're attached to your family.

The self-cherishing and self-grasping — they are unequivocally destructive to the Maras. Destroying them just destroys the Maras. And so that's why they come out in hordes, because destroying them is what actually destroys our samsara, right? The other delusions don't actually free us of samsara. It's actually destroying those two delusions that our samsara gets destroyed. Anyway, thank you very much. Lovely. Sumit and then Fran, yes.

practiceReports.speaker: Sumit
practiceReports.text:
So last Thursday I said something in a class that upset a long-time student. And they emailed me and were upset by what I said, and they basically said I'm not coming anymore.

The practice was the Vajradaka purification. And one of the things Kadam Kyle said at the end was like, now you really have to feel and believe it worked. And I was really able to do that and really feel and believe it. And my little insight on why that is the case — it's not just that I practiced it, but it's like I've been into Vajradaka practice and taken refuge in Vajradaka over the years. And I thought a lot about Wan and his particular refuge with Green Tara, for example — that's like an inspiration to me in my heart, in terms of taking refuge in Buddhas.

And my little point on it is that it's like exponential growth. When we practice things, some things are exponential — some things are not. And refuge, to me, seems very exponential growth oriented. Meaning we have to get into it even when there are imperceptible benefits, and then the benefits get huge. And then it's very easy to develop the faith.

And last night I got an email from this person. She's an elderly lady. And she emailed me at 12:37 a.m. and said that she had felt resolute — not just intellectually, but in her heart — that no matter what I said, she's not going to come back. She said that. And then she said, no, I'm going to come back. And everything like that. And it was really like, really powerful. It was like, Buddha Vajradaka can. And I just really felt this strong thing of refuge. Like Buddha did something here. And that's the power of refuge.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, that is amazing, Sumit. Thank you very much. It's like taking something that was so — like the thing you would want the least. Like a dear student being offended or hurt by something that was said, which you never want in a million years. They decided to not come back. They're like a core student. Heart-wrenching for a teacher, right? Like really a dagger.

And then you really went for refuge. You put a practice in, right? Really like from the depths of your heart. And it was like you really took steps — this, this, this, this. I'm going to solve this problem. And it usually doesn't happen like this, where it's so quick and beautiful. But you're right — Sumit, John, Mary, whoever can't solve the problems. But Buddha can. And doors will open and walls will disappear through our refuge. And it's amazing, because the Buddhas are aligned with emptiness. So emptiness, everything is possible. So thank you so much. It's an incredibly delightful resolution. It doesn't always happen that way, but it's very nice when it does. Thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
My practice continues to be Heart Jewel and Lamrim with the meditations from the New Meditation Handbook. And I've been doing them as much as I can, most days, first thing in the morning, which was my new goal. And it continues to make a tremendous difference. I'm starting to feel like I actually have a practice. That it's not just a commitment, and it's not just an activity or something that I do — that it's really becoming a practice that I look forward to.

And I'm through the 21 meditations and I'm up to number 7 now, again. And I'm like, it was only 21 days ago that I read this and it's like brand new again. So that's been great. It's really opened up a lot of space for me to deal with my discouragement issue.

And I really appreciate all the Maras, the demons that everybody drew for me. The one that hit me the most — and they've all been great — and I do recognize now more and more that Maras are coming up. Grady put in the word “courage” and “confidence” in there. And though the word discouragement has “courage” in it, I never really made that association — that what I need to do is be brave. And there have been things in my life recently that have required bravery and I've been pretty successful with that. And to take that skill that I've been honing and my practice and apply it to the discouragement and recognize it as the Maras — it's been great. So the reliance on Sangha was really great for the visualizations.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, it's fantastic, Fran. It was a very good example of relying on Sangha. That practice of relying on Sangha is a very active thing. And it's nice — when we're working through delusion, we do our part of coming up with our practice, talking to the Buddhas and our spiritual guide. But it's so important to bring in our Sangha friends into the mix. It's like, come on in! Let's do this together!

And you were obviously really open, which is a part of relying on Sangha. It's not just asking for help, as we might know. The definition of relying on Sangha is receiving help from Sangha. It's not asking — it's receiving it. Which means we have to be open. And you were so clearly open, and I think that's like the blessing.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text: I was just so, so amazed with the practice last night of Vajradaka. For one thing in particular, and it was during the time that we were reciting the mantra. I was just like in it. And I was feeling very calm and in the presence of the Buddhas. But when I looked and heard Juliana next to me, I was just blown away. Because she was practicing and reciting the mantra from her heart. And I felt her really in the practice. And it just was the best. And that's it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thank you, Mimi. That's perfect. Perfect length, too. But it's nice — even with something like that, right? You can say, like, what I practiced. And what you do, you practice rejoicing, right? It's just so important for us to connect to that, because that's what you're doing. You're rejoicing. That's why it was such a beautiful moment — because not everyone would rejoice, right? So it's like, okay, this is what happened and I practiced rejoicing. And you're right, that's a huge object of rejoicing. And it's very touching. Yeah, thank you very much. Kristen and then Anne, yes, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Kristen
practiceReports.text:
So this week I was really practicing identifying my problems — what I experience as my problems — and linking it to self-cherishing. And I feel like a lot of what feels like a problem lately is a feeling that I can't quite do anything well enough or as well as I would like. I feel a bit stretched thin. I want to do the best I can for the kids, I want to do the best I can for my patients. I currently have a student that I'm working closely with in addition to a bunch of other staff that I'm mentoring. And it feels like a bit too much, and so therefore I feel like I'm not doing any of it as well as I'd like.

And so I was really reflecting on how that's really identification with a non-existent, self-limited person that does not exist. And that if I could identify with my Buddha nature that has limitless potential to help, that would be much better. I also did some reading in Joyful Path about the disadvantages of self-cherishing. And I feel like it gets a little bit confusing sometimes — like even some of the examples in the book, it was talking about a mouse getting caught in a trap because they went after the cheese, and the fish biting on the hook because of the bait. And it's like, the mouse and the fish, they're doing that because they're hungry. And it's because they've taken a rebirth as a samsaric being. So it ended up being a little bit of a slide into renunciation. But that has been my practice this week.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Lovely, yeah, thank you, Kristen. That's a really nice example. It's like, that's exactly what we're talking about — really trying to find a problem that particularly bothers us and spelling it out like that. And it's nice, like that's something that's really close to your heart, right? You have a lot of things to do, you have high standards, you just really want to do them all to the best of your ability. You don't want to do anything halfway. But it is literally impossible to do all the things you have to do right now fully and perfectly, because there's too many things in an ordinary body and mind to do all those things perfectly.

So it's a great example. Like, oh, I feel frustrated, I can't do all the things I want to do perfectly. And even feeling the pain of that and the frustration with that, and then turning it on its head. It's like, who can do all these jobs perfectly? There's only one person who can do all these jobs perfectly, and that's Buddha. Buddha me. Buddha version of me. It's like, ah, the self-cherishing mind is preventing me from cherishing the body and mind of a Buddha. It's actually making me cherish a body and mind of someone who can't do all these things perfectly, because it's impossible to do all the things you need to do perfectly in an ordinary, deluded body and mind.

So the thing I actually want is to do everything perfectly. There's only one body and mind that can do everything perfectly — that's a Buddha's body and mind. So the self-cherishing mind is actually preventing me from identifying with the person who can actually get this job done. And then all of a sudden we're like, yeah, you're out of here. Get out of here, self-cherishing.

And as you said, it is related to renunciation. Which is like, this is how I often do the meditation too. It makes me see the contradiction — as long as I'm identifying with a samsaric body and mind, I'll be stuck with contradictory wishes. This is a really good example, Kristen. It's a really nice example of choosing a good problem that feels very real, that's very connected to the self-cherishing mind. Doing some little reading, whatever. And then thinking, okay, I want to get you out of here. It will dovetail into renunciation quite naturally, because the object of the self-cherishing mind is the samsaric body and mind. So they're very close, ultimately. Yeah, thanks so much.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne K
practiceReports.text:
I think the practice that helped me most this week was relabeling. So with my new little job, I was remembering that my first, my real identity is like friend of the world, right? And so it's a challenging new thing, but I kept remembering, like, this is not my boss, this is my friend. These are not my new coworkers, these are my friends.

But what really helped me the most was — it's an awful thing in journalism that you refer to the people you interview as your “sources.” Like their whole utility exists in terms of, can they give you the information you need for your story right now? And that's a horrible experience, to try to be extracting information to make your story better.

So I decided I was just going to go in and be their friend first. And if they had a difficult story, just be friendly with them and supportive. Or if I was interviewing an expert, just tell them how much I admire their expertise and how lovely they were. And it just lightened up my job. It lightened up the week so much. It made it so much more fun. It wasn't easy, but taking that approach of being the person's friend first, being on their side and not on the side of my story — really made it fun.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thanks so much. Relabeling is a great way to deal with self-cherishing mind — just change how we label others. And I see you practiced cherishing others. Yeah, it's a good reminder that basically there's only a few intervention points in our mind that we can ever make things move.

Think about it like upstream, downstream. Downstream are like the actual states of mind we develop — positive, negative, etc. We can't really make them happen out of nothing, right? They're downstream of only a few little things that we can possibly do. It's what we pay attention to — that's what we can control, definitely. Or how we pay attention to something, we can always intervene there. It's how we label things — and in this case, “friend.” Somewhat we can work on the intention. And then there's basically what we're mindful of. There's not many other places we can intervene immediately. They then lead downstream to virtuous states of mind that we can then utilize and benefit from.

Like if you think of a waterfall — and all the different states of mind we have, they're like at the pool at the bottom. Those are like the compounded minds: love and compassion and respect for others and so on. And then at the top there's like just four little spouts. And they are: attention, discrimination (which is like what we're labeling), intention (just somewhat, it's harder than the other three), and then mindfulness (what we're remembering). And it's like, yeah, we have to turn on one of those spouts to get things moving. And then once it's moving, then we can develop the compound minds.

So we can't just jump to cherishing others. We have to change either what we're paying attention to, what we're labeling, what our intention is, or what we're mindful of — what we're remembering. That opens up one of those little spouts and then a mind of cherishing others will arise, like in that pool.

This is just a long-winded way to say — when we're practicing Dharma, we want to be thinking about this. Like, what's the intervention point that I can get into? A lot of times we get into trouble because we're standing at the bottom of the pool going, where's the love? Where's the compassion? Where are all these delusions coming from? Come on! Go away, delusions! Come on, compassion! And what we really need to do is trot up to the top of the waterfall and start working on some of those spouts. Those are the only little intervention points that we can actually get into.

So this is a good example, right? You can't just jump to cherishing others instantly. But you can start by just labeling “friend.” That's the discrimination part. Even if you don't mean it. And then eventually, doing it over and over, the spout will completely open up and the water will flow.

practiceReports.speaker: Jose
practiceReports.text:
So the last couple of weeks I've been putting a little more emphasis on the offering part of my meditations. And I think the things that Kadam Kyle offered a couple of weeks ago about how to do the practice of offering really, really helped. Making it fast, connecting to the merit, and trying to connect with the feeling. And that part specifically — I think that was very helpful in trying to connect on how Buddha is feeling about the offering that I'm doing. I think that part really helped me to connect with the practice, and that's been very joyful.

And I guess it's kind of a question — but it kind of feels like a tantric practice in disguise, or like a mini tantric practice. Because in a sense you are imagining how Buddha feels about the offering, and in a sense you're getting the feeling. So it kind of feels like cheating to get into a tantric practice. So that's been a very good practice the last couple of weeks.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thanks, Jose. So you're remembering the three things we're trying to remember to improve our practice of offerings: remembering the benefits, or like what we're kind of getting from it; vastness; and then remembering the delight that the Buddhas receive. Remembering that the definition of offering is that which delights the Buddhas. So always connecting to and feeling their delight, just imagining to the best of your ability. And that part particularly helped you.

And then you said it's kind of like a tantric practice in disguise, and it's true. Basically everything is a tantric practice in disguise. And that's how Geshe-la has taught the teachings — everything is from the point of view of Highest Yoga Tantra. So if you look at any teaching, at some point we'll see, ah, this is like a tantric practice in disguise.

Like equanimity — it's a tantric practice in disguise. We're looking at how to view everyone in the same way so that one day we can see everyone in the same way as emptiness, or as Vajrayogini. Equanimity level one is friend, enemy, stranger — moving everyone into the friend bucket. Equanimity level seventeen or something is put everyone in the Vajrayogini bucket. This is one practice: equanimity.

So we can start to see this depth in every single practice. And we'll appreciate this over time more and more and more. And it's really actually quite delightful to discover these connections, because it makes us appreciate the ingenuity of the presentation. Like, a tantric master — okay, I'm going to teach this at the level of sutra so everyone can practice it, but it's seeding the realizations of tantra from day one. Which is incredible. Yeah, thank you.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Alright, let's get into prostration. We'll be asking this question again — like, what is the problem that prostration will solve for us? And so each one of us can kind of think about that a little bit as we go through this section.

So, page 72. “Prostration. The second preliminary limb of practice is to offer prostration or homage to the supreme beings. This is a vast practice and Shantideva summarizes it as follows:”

“With limitless verses of harmonious praise, I will glorify the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, possessors of oceans of excellence. In clouds of gentle songs of praise extolling their good qualities, as bodies always ascend to the assembly of superiors.”

“With bodies as numerous as the number of atoms in all the Buddha lands, I prostrate to the enlightened beings of three times, to Dharma, to the supreme Sangha community. I also prostrate to the bases for generating bodhichitta, to the stupas containing sacred relics, to all the learned abbots and preceptors, and to all the practitioners who have entered the path leading to liberation.”

“Shantideva specifically mentions two types of prostration here: verbal and physical. Other texts specify a third type — mental prostration, which refers to the attitude of respect and faith we extend towards worthy objects. Praises given to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth make up prostrations of speech, while physical prostrations are of many types. In the most beneficial form of practice, all three forms of prostration are performed simultaneously.”

“As for physical prostrations, there are two methods in common use. The first of these is called the half-length prostration and is performed by kneeling down and touching both hands and our forehead to the ground. The complete full-length prostration requires that our whole outstretched body be in contact with the ground. Detailed instructions on the techniques and benefits of these practices were taught by Buddha Shakyamuni and commented on by later pandits, and descriptions of the full-length prostration can be found in Stalks in Array Sutra. Offering prostration was a major practice of many great Indian pandits. The famous master Naropa, who was Marpa's principal guru and the disseminator of profound yogic methods still practiced today, used prostrations as his chief external method for accumulating merit.”

That's very nice to know.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
I think it becomes a little bit more clear as we go through the text. But the practice of just holding our hands at our heart is also a completely perfect prostration. So there comes a point in every single person's life — unless they die of a random accident — where that's the only way that they can physically prostrate anymore. And it's a point that will happen for all of us one day. Maybe we're there, maybe it's tomorrow, maybe it's in 50 years. But that will come to all of us. That's all we can do. But it's not deficient in any way. It's not lesser than. It's a completely perfect prostration. I'm saying it's all we can do because we just can't do the other two types. But I'm not saying it like it's deficient. It's a completely qualified prostration.

I just wanted to make that clear because it's not overtly obvious right at this point, because the text has just talked about the half-length and whole-length prostrations. It's explained in a little bit more detail in a second. But at that point, if anyone has questions about the actual form, I'm very happy to address any of those and demonstrate, if need be. Because we don't get a chance to look at this too often, so it's just good to make sure we're all 100% clear on prostration form.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
“The practice of prostrations has great power to purify our non-virtue and accumulate positive meritorious energy.” Those are some problems that we might have — lots of non-virtue that needs purifying, or a need for positive meritorious energy.

“But whether or not this actually happens depends solely on our mind. If we approach this practice with a pure motivation, wishing to overcome our false sense of pride and keep the qualities of the three supreme jewels of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha uppermost in our mind, it is definite that beneficial effects will follow. It is said that as a result of this practice, we will be reborn into a high-ranking family, endowed with an attractive and healthy body, and become the object of others' respect. There's even a tradition that says that the merit we gain from paying homage in this way is equal to the number of atoms in the ground covered by our prostrate body.”

So tall people are better off than other people. Sorry, short people — get less merit, I guess. I should use this phrase: there isn't even a tradition of saying that. That helps you get motivated. Cool. But if it doesn't, don't worry as much about that benefit.

So this idea of doing it with a pure motivation just means not totally doing it as a workout. Like, it has to have some kind of spiritual component. It doesn't have to be perfect and absolutely focused, but not like I'm doing some jumping jacks. It's not that common, but it can become that, because it is actually incredibly blissful eventually to get into the groove of prostrations. And very physically beneficial. It is easy to make it like an awesome free workout at some point. But we should always want to make sure it's a spiritual practice.

There's another problem that this solves that's keyed in here: “wishing to overcome our false sense of pride.” So that's one of the benefits of it. A friend of mine said, when she does prostrations, because she has this issue with pride, she says she thinks to the Buddhas and to her spiritual guide, “May I be like the rug underneath your feet.” And thinks that like every time she prostrates. Which is offensive to our self-cherishing mind. But it's a beautiful, humble attitude — may I be the very rug beneath your feet. Like the self is nothing. So that would be a good problem to solve. And prostrations has the effect of developing humility, which is very, very useful.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
“What is the exact method for performing prostrations? There are various traditions of practice, even within Mahayana Buddhism. According to one widely followed tradition, we begin by standing erect and placing the palms of our hand together in an attitude of prayer. The thumbs touching and tucked inside the palms to symbolize a wish-fulfilling jewel.”

“It should be noted that merely to hold our hands in this or similar gesture of respect, or even to bow our heads slightly, qualifies as a physical prostration. It is not necessary to touch the ground at all.”

“We then touch our folded hands to four places on our body to plant the seeds to attain various qualities of an enlightened being. First we touch the top of our head, in order to attain a Buddha's ushnisha — the crown protuberance that results from paying respect to our spiritual guide.”

There's a problem — so if we don't have a lot of faith or respect for our spiritual guide, I'm starting to create the cause for that from a prostration. Which symbolizes a Buddha's inner realizations.

“Then touch our forehead, throat, and heart in order to attain a Buddha's hair curl — a sign of wisdom.” So we have ignorance — and this will solve our ignorance problem. “Power of speech, and power of mind respectively. If our motivation and faith are strong, following these practices will place powerful potentialities in our mind stream for our future attainment of a Buddha's transcendent body, speech, and mind. After touching these four places, we then bend down to do a half-length or full-length prostration and then immediately stand up again. We repeat this process at least three times and then always finish by touching our folded hands to our crown, forehead, throat, and heart.”

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
“Offering prostrations was a very well-known practice throughout Tibet. Je Tsongkhapa stressed the importance of this practice, and during a retreat with several of his principal disciples performed three and a half million full-length prostrations.”

Yeah, famously he eroded the ground — there was like a little ditch in the ground where he was prostrating, just from his skin rubbing the rock enough times.

“Another great Tibetan teacher, Jampa Rinpoche, who is said to be a manifestation of Maitreya Buddha, claimed to limit his external methods of accumulating merit to just two practices every day: offering one hundred water bowls and making one hundred prostrations.”

Yeah — who needs a job at the Dharma Center? That's all you need to do to accumulate enough merit, if you did it with a pure enough mind. If you did it with a pure enough mind, it's completely sufficient.

“Even into old age he continued this practice. He was very tall, and because he would cover so much ground with his body, he was able to accumulate much merit from his practice. One day he exclaimed, ‘How wonderful it would be if I were even taller, and then I could accumulate even more merit!’”

mainTeaching.speaker: Fran
mainTeaching.text: So this refers to doing the touching the four places with bending. But I've seen people, and I was told by somebody else, that when we're just standing — we're not actually bending — that that's not something that we should be doing. I've seen it done like that, where people are standing and doing the four body touches. And I've seen them not do it. So is there a correct or incorrect in that?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah. The tradition is that when you do the full-length prostration and the half-length prostration, then you touch those four places. And then if you do a prostration where you keep your hands at your heart, then you don't need to do that.

To me, it's almost like when we just do this, it gives us this freedom to really do the mental prostrating part better. Because we don't have to do anything else. Because when we do prostrations, we try to imagine infinite bodies prostrating for infinite eons, which is quite a big thing to do with your mind. And when you're doing the half-length and the full-length physical prostrations, you can do that with your mind, but it takes quite a bit of concentration.

So to me, when I'm in a situation where I can't do a half-length or full-length prostration — like if I'm in a big event and I'm sitting in chairs where I can't bend down, or it wouldn't be appropriate — I just think, this is an amazing opportunity to do the mental part really, really well. And just let my imagination go wild. It's a little bit of a privilege, actually, in some ways, to really get skilled at that.

So yeah, that's generally the tradition. I don't think anyone's going to break someone's finger for touching their forehead and crown and so on when they're standing. But generally speaking, those are three ways to do it: just this, or the half-length, or the full-length.

mainTeaching.speaker: Ryan
mainTeaching.text: So let's say I'm sitting on the train or even on my back and I want to just do this. What's the simplest way I do this? Because there's a lot of words here in the text. What is the simplest way to make a mental prostration? What's the words I'm using mentally?

mainTeaching.speaker: Ryan
mainTeaching.text: I prostrate my body to the Buddha, with the goal to destroy self-cherishing, or to gain humility, or to destroy deluded pride.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: That's it. Sounds good, yeah. Lovely, thank you.

mainTeaching.speaker: David
mainTeaching.text: I had never seen this phrase — “or even to bow our head slightly qualifies as a physical prostration.” I was wondering if maybe it might be appropriate in certain times when you're trying to act according to the inclinations of others or something like that. It sounds like it's not one of the three kind of traditional prostrations, but curious if you had any thoughts about that.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah. And later it gets into this a little bit. But this is what we're going to emphasize in the second class. But when Geshe-la has taught about this as a practical tool to use in daily life, he especially taught on that to prostrate means to respect others. Which is a big area of investigation, right? How much do I respect others, and what does it mean to really respect someone? Not just be with someone, not just be nice to someone, but to respect them. And there's a difference — there's an elevation of that person when we respect them. It's not putting up with them or whatever. It's really respecting them.

So the idea of bowing your head slightly — it's like showing a physical gesture of respect which is appropriate for the society that we're in. In some societies it might be to literally bow, like at our hip, because that's the sign of respect in certain societies. Or there might be some other form from where we're from or what we do or what culture we're in that is the right way. And that's kind of the meaning there. It's like — do some physical showing of respect to the other, something that would lower you and raise them in some way, or show that we're being humble.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
I remember once there was someone who came from one of those cultures, came to the temple. And he was the father of a regular member there, and he'd come on and off for a few years. And he would always prostrate to a dear friend of mine. And my friend would wave to him. And this happened a bit. And then one day she was in the cafe there and he prostrated to her, and she waved to him. And then he screamed at her for a very long time. And basically he was so deeply offended that she was not prostrating to him back. It was like the sign of an incredible offense.

She cried, because it felt very hurtful. And I'm not saying he's right. But as bodhisattvas — trainee bodhisattvas — we're always thinking, how can I fit in with society and what other people's norms are so that I can benefit them? We're not trying to impose our own moral judgments on them and making them fit into it.

There was another person like that in the teacher training program that I did in England. And I was very huggy at the time. I was hugging everyone. So I'd always hug him. And he's from a very different culture. And then one day he said to me very politely, “Let's talk about the things that we think each other can improve.” Okay, let's talk about that. I don't have anything for you. “Okay, what do you have for me?” He said, “In my culture, when someone hugs someone else, it is like, in your culture, when someone kisses someone with their tongue.” And I said, thank you. I'm very sorry. I didn't understand.

And it was just this great teaching — it was imposing my thing without any care or respect for him on him. From one point of view, I didn't mean anything by it. But from another point of view, there was a little negligence there, right? Not really thinking or even just asking, “Hey, is it okay?” He would have said, “No, please do not hug me. Please don't touch me.”

So this point about respect and this gesture — sometimes it's just a little bow of the head, or maybe there's something else that's culturally appropriate. It's nice to think about this, right? How can I use my body to respect others?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Okay, let's stop there. So in the next class we'll be talking about how this mind of respect is key to the practice of prostration — how can we train in respect for others. And so again, we'll be thinking about how is a mind of respect something that solves my daily problems.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text:
Just a reminder — we're off next Sunday because of the U.S. Festival, because we'll be learning about the Heart Sutra. Reminder that it is online, so if you can't go in person but you want to connect to teachings on the Heart Sutra from Gen Khenrab and get those blessings of realizing emptiness, you can join in. And it will be both live, or if you can't do it live, you can always just watch it when it's recorded. It would be very nice.

And then in May we have our Walk for All Peace, which is I think the 17th — Sunday the 17th. If you're around, please do come. Invite a friend or two. The world needs peace. And it will be a lovely event. And even if you're anti-walking, there is a special job of setting up a picnic blanket or two in Brooklyn Bridge Park and just basically setting up a blanket there and sitting there until we come, so we can have a little picnic there. So if you are interested in somehow being involved but the idea of going for a walk is either dreadful or not accessible, that's a job.

There is TTP that day. I know it's a little bit a lot for one day. But because of the Festival, and then we have OSG, and then there's Memorial Day weekend — there's just a lot of off days. So we did want to offer it that day. Encourage to rally if you got it in you. Have an extra cup of coffee that day. Or two.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text:
Okay, let's dedicate here. And then we'll come back at 6:10.

We can think — through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications.

Okay, thanks everyone. See you in a bit. Thank you.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Anyone have any final ideas about specifically how we could practice prostration and/or respecting others in the week ahead, two weeks ahead? David, yeah?

conclusion.speaker: David
conclusion.text: Ryan and I were talking about really keying in to people's sufferings and their problems and viewing those as very important — more important than our own — and that particular aspect of respecting others, I think, could be very powerful.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Yeah, that's a really nice one. It's like respecting how hard someone's working to deal with their problems and challenges. And that's really those unseen battles that we don't know everyone's fighting all the time. And sometimes if we don't see other attributes that seem easy to appreciate, it's often because they're fighting really hard. Fighting some demons or some pain or some sickness or some whatever. And the fight is actually admirable — that they can keep fighting and they have that inner strength to fight those battles every day. And that's something we can really respect in people. Because maybe we don't do that or have to do that right now. Yeah, it's a great idea. It's a really, really nice way to get into that mind of respect. Thank you.

conclusion.speaker: Fran
conclusion.text: Jose and I were talking about having difficulties respecting certain people and realizing that that's just our own self-cherishing that prevents us from respecting them. And to stop viewing them as that person that we normally see — that inherently unrespectable person.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Yeah, definitely. Bring in a little emptiness practice in there. Dissolving the unrespectable person we normally see. Because they don't exist, for sure.

conclusion.speaker: Marianne
conclusion.text: We talked about having problems respecting people that we don't respect. And Kristen suggested thinking of them as our teachers. And that specifically, they're very specifically training us for something. And if they are trying to take advantage of us, that's just sort of part of our training — to not let them do something that's bad for everybody.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Yeah, that's a great idea. Just using that practice of viewing others as our teacher. And then even if it's some bad behavior that we need to stand up to, it's like, okay, they're teaching me how to become someone who can stand up to people's bad behavior. And who has the courage to stand up to that.

I think that's nice. That's a great way to respect others. Anything else before we wrap it up? Okay, well thank you all so much. Either see you all in the Pure Land or see you in this Pure Land in a couple weeks.

closingPrayer.text: Prayer of the Virtuous Tradition So that the tradition of Je Tsongkhapa, the King of the Dharma, may flourish, may all obstacles be pacified and may all favorable conditions abound. Through the two collections of myself and others gathered throughout the three times, may the doctrine of Conqueror Losang Dragpa flourish forevermore.
